question: How will a front-tire flat typically feel to the rider, and why is it particularly hazardous?
choice_a: It has no noticeable effect on steering
choice_b: The steering will feel "heavy," and it is hazardous because it affects your steering, requiring careful control to keep your balance
choice_c: The rear of the motorcycle jerks or sways from side to side
explanation: If the front tire goes flat, the steering will feel "heavy." A front-wheel flat is particularly hazardous because it affects your steering, and you have to steer well to keep your balance.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.34, 'Tire Failure'

question: How will a rear-tire flat typically feel to the rider?
choice_a: The steering will feel unusually heavy
choice_b: There is no perceptible difference from a front flat
choice_c: The back of the motorcycle may jerk or sway from side to side
explanation: If the rear tire goes flat, the back of the motorcycle may jerk or sway from side to side.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.34, 'Tire Failure'

question: If either tire goes flat while riding, what should you do?
choice_a: Immediately apply both brakes as hard as possible
choice_b: Accelerate to reach a repair shop faster
choice_c: Let go of the handlebars and coast
choice_d: Hold the handgrips firmly, ease off the throttle, keep a straight course, and if braking is needed, gradually apply the brake of the tire that isn't flat
explanation: If either tire goes flat while riding, hold the handgrips firmly, ease off the throttle, and keep a straight course; if braking is required, gradually apply the brake of the tire that isn't flat, if you're sure which one it is, then edge to the side of the road, squeeze the clutch, and stop.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.34, 'Tire Failure'

question: If the throttle sticks, what is the correct first step, and what should you do if it remains stuck?
choice_a: Try twisting the throttle back and forth to free the cable; if it stays stuck, operate the engine cut-off switch and squeeze the clutch at the same time
choice_b: Immediately turn off the ignition key while at speed
choice_c: Accelerate harder to try to break the stuck cable free
explanation: If the situation allows, twist the throttle back and forth several times to try to free a stuck cable; if the throttle stays stuck, immediately operate the engine cut-off switch and squeeze the clutch lever at the same time to remove power from the rear wheel.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.34-35, 'Stuck Throttle'

question: What is a "wobble," and what commonly causes it?
choice_a: A slow, gentle drift that only occurs above 100 mph
choice_b: A sudden side-to-side shaking of the front wheel and handlebars, most often traced to improper loading, unsuitable accessories, or incorrect tire pressure
choice_c: A normal and harmless vibration that requires no attention
choice_d: A problem that only affects three-wheel motorcycles
explanation: A "wobble" occurs when the front wheel and handlebars suddenly start to shake from side to side at any speed; most wobbles can be traced to improper loading, unsuitable accessories, or incorrect tire pressure.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.35, 'Wobble'

question: What should a rider do -- and NOT do -- if a wobble occurs?
choice_a: Try to accelerate out of the wobble to stabilize it
choice_c: Grip the handlebars firmly without fighting the wobble, and close the throttle gradually without applying the brakes
choice_d: Let go of the handlebars completely
explanation: Trying to accelerate out of a wobble will only make the motorcycle more unstable. Instead, grip the handlebars firmly but don't fight the wobble, and close the throttle gradually to slow down -- do not apply the brakes, since braking could make the wobble worse.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.35, 'Wobble'

question: What happens if a motorcycle's drive chain or belt breaks while riding?
choice_b: Nothing changes; the motorcycle continues normally
choice_c: The front wheel immediately locks up
choice_d: There is an instant loss of power to the rear wheel; close the throttle and brake to a stop in a safe area
explanation: If the chain or belt breaks, you'll notice an instant loss of power to the rear wheel; close the throttle and brake to a stop in a safe area.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.35, 'Drive Train Problems'

question: What usually causes an engine to "lock" or "freeze" (engine seizure)?
choice_a: The engine is usually low on oil, causing moving parts to bind and the engine to overheat
choice_b: Too much oil in the engine
explanation: When the engine "locks" or "freezes" it is usually low on oil; the engine's moving parts can't move smoothly against each other and the engine overheats. Squeeze the clutch lever to disengage the engine, pull off the road, and check the oil.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.35, 'Engine Seizure'

question: What does the manual recommend if you are in traffic and an animal darts into your path?
choice_a: Always swerve out of your lane regardless of surrounding traffic
choice_b: Remain in your lane, since hitting something small is less dangerous than hitting something big like a car
choice_d: Slam on both brakes regardless of the animal's size
explanation: You should do everything you safely can to avoid hitting an animal, but if you are in traffic, remain in your lane -- hitting something small is less dangerous to you than hitting something big, like a car.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.35-36, 'Animals'

question: If a rider is being chased by a dog, what does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Kick the animal away as you pass
choice_b: Stop completely until the dog loses interest
choice_c: Downshift, approach the animal slowly, then accelerate and leave it behind, without kicking at it
choice_d: Swerve sharply around the dog at full speed
explanation: Motorcycles seem to attract dogs. If chased, downshift and approach the animal slowly, then accelerate and leave the animal behind -- don't kick at it, and keep control of your motorcycle while looking where you want to go.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.36, 'Animals'

question: What should a rider do when encountering a large animal such as a deer, elk, or cattle?
choice_a: Accelerate to pass before it moves
choice_b: Sound the horn and continue at the same speed
choice_c: Swerve into the oncoming lane immediately
choice_d: Brake and prepare to stop, since large animals are unpredictable
explanation: For larger animals (deer, elk, cattle), brake and prepare to stop -- they are unpredictable.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.36, 'Animals'

question: If your face protection is struck by a flying object such as an insect or pebble, what should you do?
choice_a: Keep your eyes on the road and hands on the handlebars, and pull off the road when safe to repair the damage
choice_b: Immediately remove your helmet while riding
choice_c: Close your eyes momentarily to avoid debris
choice_d: Swerve hard to shake off the object
explanation: If face protection gets smeared or cracked by a flying object, keep your eyes on the road and your hands on the handlebars; when safe, pull off the road and repair the damage.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.36, 'Flying Objects'

question: Before turning onto the roadside to rest or check your motorcycle, what should you check first?
choice_a: Nothing; any roadside surface is safe at any speed
choice_b: That the roadside surface is firm enough to ride on -- slow way down if it's soft grass, loose sand, or you're unsure
choice_d: Whether other riders are already stopped there
explanation: If you need to leave the road, check the roadside first -- make sure the surface is firm enough to ride on; if it's soft grass, loose sand, or you're just not sure, slow way down before turning onto it.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.36, 'Getting Off the Road'

question: Why should a rider signal clearly before pulling off the road to rest or check the motorcycle?
choice_a: Signaling is only required when turning back onto the road
choice_b: It has no real safety benefit
choice_c: Drivers behind might not expect the rider to slow down and change direction
explanation: Signal clearly, since drivers behind might not expect you to slow down; check your mirror and make a head check before you take any action.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.36, 'Getting Off the Road'
